title: CERN 2027 Prep
subtitle: Summer Student + openlab · summer 2027
description: A 22-week programme in two phases: a sprint to the 21 January deadline, then the advanced work that makes you useful on day one. Lessons with exercises, recall that keeps them, drills written from memory, timed checkpoints and five real projects.

labels.projectsIntro: Five real projects, built step by step across the weeks. Each step is done when its proof is in: a link, a measured number, a pasted output.

phases.title: Phase 1 · Application sprint
phases.goal: By 21 January: two finished projects with tests and CI on GitHub, a first ML result on real physics data, the basics of C++, Python, the shell and Git written from memory, and both applications submitted.

phases.title: Phase 2 · Day-one ready
phases.goal: By mid-April: fast, parallel C++; deep learning from training to a quantised, deployed model; a monitored service on Kubernetes; an open-source contribution; and a five-minute talk about all of it.

projects.title: Project 1 · Dimuon spectrum and resonance masses
projects.what: Python analysis of 100,000 real CMS collisions: invariant mass, fitted masses with uncertainties, tests and CI.

projects.title: Project 2 · Event processor in C++
projects.what: The same measurement in modern C++ with CMake, unit tests, sanitizers and a benchmark. Made fast and parallel in phase 2.

projects.title: Project 3 · Higgs and jet classifiers
projects.what: Boosted trees on simulated Higgs events, then a PyTorch network, quantised and exported for fast inference.

projects.title: Project 4 · Model service on Kubernetes
projects.what: The jet tagger as an HTTP service in a container: three replicas on a cluster, updated under load, broken on purpose, monitored with an alert, and measured.

projects.title: Project 5 · Open-source contribution
projects.what: One real pull request to a scientific project: chosen with measurements, small, tested, explained and followed up.

94 CHF per day, health insurance, travel help

facts.title: openlab Summer Student Programme

pages.note: **Check the date on CERN's own page.** The 21 January date comes from the 2027 job listings. The official openlab page didn't show a date yet when this plan was made, and its apply link still pointed at 2026. Confirm on the [CERN careers portal](https://careers.cern/) and the [openlab page](https://openlab.cern/cern-openlab-summer-student-programme) before you submit.
pages.intro: Both calls ask for a CV, one academic reference letter less than 12 months old, your latest official transcript and an enrolment certificate, as clearly labelled PDFs in English or French. You upload the reference letter yourself, so ask early. For openlab a motivation letter is recommended, not required. Write one anyway and name the area you want.

quiz.q: What is the core idea of RAII?
o: A resource's lifetime is tied to an object's lifetime
quiz.why: The destructor releases what the constructor acquired, so cleanup is automatic.

quiz.q: A std::unique_ptr can be…

quiz.q: A particle flies out exactly perpendicular to the beam. Its pseudorapidity η is…

quiz.q: When does a base class need a virtual destructor?
o: When a derived object is deleted through a base pointer
quiz.why: Otherwise only the base destructor runs and the derived part leaks.

quiz.q: A ROOT TTree is mainly used to…
quiz.why: Each entry is an event and each branch a variable, stored column-wise.

quiz.q: What is a container in Docker?
o: A running instance of an image
quiz.why: The Dockerfile builds an image; running the image gives a container.

quiz.q: You count 400 events in a bin. Its statistical uncertainty is about…
quiz.why: √400 = 20, which is a relative uncertainty of 5%.

quiz.q: In NumPy, a[a > 5] gives…
o: The elements of a that are greater than 5
quiz.why: a > 5 makes a boolean mask, and indexing with a mask keeps the elements where it is True.

quiz.q: A merge stops with a conflict. After editing the file, what completes the merge?
o: git add the file, then git commit
quiz.why: Resolve the markers, stage the file with git add, and commit. git merge --continue does the same.

quiz.q: curve_fit returns popt and pcov. The one-sigma uncertainties of the parameters are…
o: The square roots of the diagonal of pcov
quiz.why: pcov is the covariance matrix. Its diagonal holds the variances, and the uncertainty is the square root of a variance.

quiz.q: In a GitHub Actions workflow, which line makes it run on every push?
quiz.why: The on: key lists the events that trigger the workflow. runs-on: picks the machine.

quiz.q: while (std::getline(file, line)) stops when…
o: The read fails, usually because the file has ended
quiz.why: getline returns the stream, which converts to false once a read fails. Empty lines are read normally.

quiz.q: A class frees memory in its destructor. What else does the rule of three say it needs?
o: A copy constructor and a copy assignment operator
quiz.why: The compiler's default copies would copy the pointer, and two objects would free the same memory.

quiz.q: Why give curve_fit starting values p0 when fitting a peak?
o: From a poor start the minimiser can stop in the wrong place or fail
quiz.why: The fit walks downhill from where it starts. Start near the peak you mean.

quiz.why: Requests under way = throughput × latency, so 60 = 1,200 × latency, which gives 0.05 seconds. It is the time spent queueing.

quiz.q: A deployment has 3 replicas, maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0. What happens first in a rolling update?

One new pod is started, and nothing is stopped until it is ready
The service is deleted and created again
quiz.why: No fewer than three may be ready, and one extra is allowed. So the capacity never drops during the update.

quiz.q: What does Kubernetes do with a pod whose readiness probe fails?
o: It stops sending it requests through the service, and leaves it running
It moves it to another node
quiz.why: Restarting is what a failing liveness probe causes. Readiness only decides whether the pod gets traffic.

quiz.q: Why does a pod sleep for a few seconds in a preStop hook before it shuts down?

To give the liveness probe time to fail

quiz.q: A new release can't start, and its pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. Why do the callers notice nothing?

quiz.why: The old pods keep serving. kubectl logs shows the cause, and kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous version.

tasks.desc: Prometheus draws one graph at a time. Run Grafana in your cluster with a deployment and a service of its own, add your Prometheus as a data source under its service name, and build a dashboard with three panels: requests per second for each pod, the p50 and p99 of the handler, and the share of each jet class.

quiz.q: A counter reads 3,481,220. What do you do with it in a query?
o: Wrap it in rate(...[1m]) to get its rise per second
Divide it by the number of pods
Reset it to zero every minute
quiz.why: The value of a counter means little. Its rate is the signal, and rate also copes with restarts that set the counter back to zero.

quiz.q: How exact is a p99 that Prometheus computes from a histogram?
o: Only as exact as the buckets are wide, because it interpolates inside the bucket that holds the rank
It is always the upper edge of the last bucket
Exact if the scrape interval is short enough
quiz.why: The histogram only knows how many observations fell into each bucket. Choose the edges around the values you expect.

quiz.q: The handler's histogram reports a p99 of 2.3 ms and the load generator a p99 of 29.9 ms for the same minutes. Why?
o: The generator counts each request twice
The histogram times the handler only, and the generator sees the whole journey: network, waiting, parsing, the handler and the way back
quiz.why: Measure latency where the caller is, and use the service's own numbers to find out where the time goes.

quiz.q: An alert rule has for: 30s. The condition has been true for 10 seconds. Which state is the alert in?
quiz.why: It is pending until the condition has held for the full 30 seconds without a break, and firing after that.

quiz.q: You have 2,000 independent files to process, at half an hour each. How do you run that at CERN?
o: As one MPI program on the HPC cluster
As 2,000 batch jobs from one HTCondor description
On your laptop over a weekend
quiz.why: Independent pieces of work are high-throughput computing. One description with queue 2000 and the job number as the argument does it.

quiz.q: Why does an analysis job on the Grid run at the site that holds its data?
o: A job description is a few kilobytes and a data set is terabytes, so moving the job is far cheaper
Only that site has the software
quiz.why: Rucio knows where the copies are, and CVMFS brings the software to whichever site runs the job.

Work on a new branch, commit and push it. Then play the maintainer, who also appends a line to the end of the README, for example the licence, and pushes it. Your rebase will stop with a conflict, because both of you changed the same place. Resolve it so that both lines stay. Finish with the forced push, the squash merge and the clean-up.

quiz.q: pyproject.toml contains the line to_onnx = "salt.onnx.to_onnx:main" under [project.scripts]. What does it say?
o: The package depends on a package called to_onnx
Installing the package creates the command to_onnx, which calls the function main in salt/onnx/to_onnx.py
The file to_onnx.py is excluded from the package
The tests are started with to_onnx
quiz.why: It is an entry point. The dots of the module are the slashes of the path, and the part behind the colon is the function.

quiz.q: A class defines training_step, and git grep finds no call of it in the whole repository. What is the explanation?
o: The class inherits from a framework class, and the framework calls the method
It is called from a YAML file
quiz.why: Inversion of control: the framework owns the loop and calls the hooks that you fill in.

quiz.q: You want to know which commit introduced a call that looks strange. Which command finds it?
quiz.why: log -S lists the commits that added or removed the text. git show --stat on the oldest of them shows what else came with it.

quiz.q: You have forked a project and cloned your fork. What are origin and upstream?
o: origin is the project, upstream is your fork
origin is your fork, upstream is the project
origin is your computer, upstream is GitHub
quiz.why: You push to origin, your fork. From upstream, the project, you only fetch.

quiz.q: After your fix the new test passes and an old test fails. What do you do?
o: Change the old test's expected value to the new result
Read the old test, decide whether it or the fix is wrong, and explain a changed test in the pull request
Add a special case so that both pass
quiz.why: A failing old test is information. Sometimes it has caught a mistake in the fix, and sometimes it passed only because of the bug.

quiz.q: You rebased the branch of your pull request and git push is rejected. Which command is right?
quiz.why: The rebased commits must replace the old ones on your fork. The lease form refuses if somebody else has pushed to the branch in the meantime.

quiz.q: Which three parts make the one-sentence message of a talk?
o: Your name, your university and your supervisor
The problem, what you did, and the number that shows it worked
The tools, the languages and the libraries
An introduction, a middle and thanks
quiz.why: A listener who keeps this one sentence has got what you came to say.

quiz.q: You measured 150 words in 75 seconds and plan four and a half minutes of speaking. How many words may the script have?

quiz.q: The rehearsal takes six minutes for a slot of five. What do you change?

quiz.q: What is on the last slide?
